Chef Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A chef resume has to prove one thing above all: that you can run a kitchen under pressure and send out food people remember. Hiring managers do not hire on a list of cuisines. They hire on consistency — plates that leave the pass on time and a team that holds together on a busy Saturday — and they check both before they ever call you.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, the skills hiring sides actually scan for, and the mistakes that quietly cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works: what you ran, who ate it, and what changed.

Quick answer: A chef resume should open with your cuisine and station experience, name the kitchens and covers you handled, show food-cost and waste control, list your certifications, and prove consistency under service pressure — then keep the layout single-column with standard headings so tracking systems parse every section cleanly.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with cuisine and covers — what you cooked, for how many, and where.
  • Prove kitchen economics with food-cost, waste, and ticket-time numbers.
  • Name the stations, cuisines, and techniques from the posting.
  • Every bullet pairs a task with a result: what you ran, who ate it, and what changed.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Kitchen Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to an executive chef or a restaurant owner and you will not hear "passionate about food." You will hear:

  • Covers and consistency. How many covers you handled, and whether the food was the same on plate one and plate two hundred — a chef who held quality across a full Saturday service beats a long list of dishes.
  • Kitchen economics. Food cost, waste, and ticket times are what chefs are judged on. "Cut food cost while holding the menu" is a hiring signal; "responsible for kitchen costs" is not.
  • Range across stations. Grill, sauté, pastry, and the pass — plus enough menu and supplier knowledge to run a kitchen without hand-holding. Name the cuisines, the stations, and the techniques you actually worked.
  • Team leadership. Training, rostering, and holding standards when the kitchen is short-staffed — hiring managers want a chef whose team still plates well when things go wrong.
  • Hygiene and safety. Clean inspection records, allergen handling, and safe storage — if your kitchen cannot pass an inspection, nothing else on the resume matters.

If your resume reads like a menu — all dishes, no kitchen — it will lose to a service record.

Chef Resume Example

Below is a complete example for an executive chef with fine-dining and high-volume experience. It is fictional — the name and figures are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: what you ran, who ate it, and what changed.

MARCUS BELL — Executive Chef
Chicago, IL · (312) 555-0186 · marcus.bell@email.com

SUMMARY
Executive chef with 9 years running high-volume and fine-dining kitchens. Led a 14-person brigade through 220-cover Saturday services with 12-minute average ticket times; cut food cost from 31% to 28% and waste by 18% in one year while holding a 4.9 guest rating. Modern American and French technique; ServSafe certified.

SKILLS
Menu development · Food-cost control · Sauté · Grill · Pastry · Butchery · Plating · Allergen management · Inventory & ordering · Supplier negotiation · Staff training · Rota planning · HACCP · ServSafe · Banquet service · Wine pairing

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Executive Chef — Ember & Oak, Chicago, IL | 2022–Present - Lead a 14-person brigade through 220-cover Saturday services, holding 12-minute average ticket times with no walkouts in two years - Cut food cost from 31% to 28% by reworking the supplier list and portioning, saving $6,400 a month while the menu stayed full - Reduced kitchen waste by 18% with a daily prep list and a nose-to-tail specials board that turned trim into sellable dishes - Rebuilt the dessert menu with the pastry team, lifting dessert orders from 1 in 5 tables to 1 in 3 within a season - Train 3 sous chefs and 6 line cooks; two of my line cooks now run their own stations unsupervised on weekends

Sous Chef — The Copper Table, Chicago, IL | 2019–2022 - Ran the pass on 160-cover Friday services, calling tickets for a 10-person line and keeping the kitchen on time through full books - Wrote the seasonal menu with the head chef, adding 8 dishes that stayed on the menu for two years - Managed ordering for a $9,000 weekly food budget, cutting stock-outs to zero across a full summer season - Covered the head chef's holidays and sick days, running the kitchen end to end with no service failures

Line Cook — Bistro Marlow, Chicago, IL | 2017–2019 - Worked grill and sauté on 120-cover services, learning the pace of a real dinner rush from the inside - Prepped the full mise en place for two stations each shift, with a zero-missed-prep record in the final year - Earned promotion to chef de partie after 14 months

EDUCATION
A.A.S., Culinary Arts — Kendall College, Chicago, IL, 2017 ServSafe Food Protection Manager Certification, 2021

Why it works: the summary leads with the two things kitchen hiring managers check first — volume under pressure (220 covers, 12-minute tickets) and kitchen economics (food cost 31% to 28%) — then names the cuisine and the certification. Every bullet pairs a task with a result: faster tickets, lower waste, a team that can run without you.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: cuisine, covers, economics

"220-cover Saturday services," "food cost from 31% to 28%," "Modern American and French" — three facts that let a hiring manager place you in thirty seconds. Lead with volume and a result, not with your training.

Experience: services with outcomes, not duties

Each bullet should answer "what changed because you ran it?" "Cooked in a busy restaurant" is a duty; "cut food cost from 31% to 28% while holding the menu" is proof. Covers, ticket times, food cost, waste, and team size are the metrics chefs are judged on — put at least three on your resume.

Stations and techniques: proof you can work the line

Your stations are the closest thing to proof a chef gets. Name the stations you actually ran — grill, sauté, pastry, the pass — and the cuisines behind them. One vague claim costs more than a missing skill — only list stations you could step onto tomorrow and run.

Skills: mirror the posting, honestly

List the cuisines and techniques you have actually cooked with, in the posting's own words — "sauté" versus "pan work" matters to filters, and so does "HACCP" versus "food safety." Do not list a cuisine you only cooked once; the trial shift will find it out. Depth in one cuisine beats a long list of half-known dishes.

Chef Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting's language exactly — "sauté" vs "pan work" matters to filters:

  • Cuisines: Modern American, French, Italian, Mediterranean, farm-to-table, seasonal
  • Stations & techniques: sauté, grill, pastry, butchery, plating, sous vide, fermentation, banquet service
  • Kitchen management: food-cost control, waste reduction, inventory & ordering, supplier negotiation, rota planning, staff training, menu development
  • Safety & standards: HACCP, ServSafe, allergen management, hygiene inspection, temperature control

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Restaurants and hotel groups screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. 5 Mistakes That Cost Chefs Interviews

  1. A menu, not a service record. A long list of dishes with no covers, ticket times, or costs reads as a cook, not a chef. Add the numbers that show you ran it.
  2. Hiding the economics. If you never mention food cost, waste, or ordering, a hiring manager assumes you never owned them. Name at least one kitchen-economics result.
  3. Duties without results. "Cooked on the line" could describe any cook. Add the result — faster tickets, lower waste, a team you trained — to every bullet.
  4. Vague cuisine claims. Listing six cuisines you barely touched fails the trial shift. List what you have actually cooked, week after week.
  5. Ignoring hygiene and safety. A resume with no mention of food safety or allergen handling tells a hiring manager your kitchen is a risk. Put your certification where it can be seen.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do chefs need a culinary degree?

No. Most kitchens hire on proof of skill — a trial shift, a record of services run, and references from chefs you worked under — rather than a degree. Culinary school, apprenticeships, and working up from line cook all count when the record is real.

What experience should a new chef put on a resume?

Lead with stations and services. A line-cook role on a busy service, a prep record, or a banquet shift all count as kitchen experience. Name what you ran, how many covers, and what changed — the same pattern as any senior bullet.

How do I show kitchen leadership on a resume?

Name the team and the service: how many cooks you led, what the covers were, and what held together under pressure. Training juniors, covering the head chef's absence, and holding standards on a short-staffed night are the proofs they look for.

Should a chef resume include photos of my food?

No — keep the resume itself text-only so tracking systems can parse it, and put food photos in a separate portfolio or social profile linked from the header. A photo inside the resume file is usually stripped or misread by the parser.

How long should a chef resume be?

One page for most chefs, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a long career across genuinely different kitchens — fine dining, banquets, hotels — and even then keep your best numbers on page one.

Can chefs work in different countries?

Yes — chefs work all over the world, and kitchens in other countries hire on the same proof: a trial shift, a service record, and references from chefs you worked under. Check the work-permit rules for the country before you apply, and keep your certifications and references ready to share.
